etymology: From the Saxon hemlic, a bitter poisonous herb of the fields. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew rosh, a bitter and venomous plant elsewhere translated gall — not the American hemlock tree, but a rank weed of the furrow.
biblical_def: Hemlock is a bitter poison that grows where it is not sown, and both prophets who use it apply it to the corruption of justice. Hosea describes a people whose word means nothing — “They have spoken words, swearing falsely in making a covenant: thus judgment springeth up as hemlock in the furrows of the field” (Hos 10:4). The picture is agricultural and precise. A furrow is prepared ground; something will grow in it. Where the covenant has been broken and oaths are sworn falsely, what comes up in the ploughed rows is not wheat but poison, and it comes up thickly, because a weed needs no cultivation. Amos states the same charge in a series of absurdities: “Shall horses run upon the rock? will one plow there with oxen? for ye have turned judgment into gall, and the fruit of righteousness into hemlock” (Amo 6:12). Horses do not gallop over bare rock and no man ploughs it with oxen — and it is exactly as unnatural, says the prophet, for a covenant nation to turn its courts into instruments of poison. Note that in neither prophet is the complaint that justice has ceased. Judgment still springeth up; there are still courts, verdicts, and covenants. What has changed is the crop. A society does not usually abolish its justice; it poisons it, and keeps the furrows.
webster_summary: A bitter and poisonous herb of the fields; in the prophets, the crop that grows in the furrows of a nation which has corrupted its justice.
webster_full: HEMLOCK, n. A poisonous plant of the genus Conium, having a bitter and narcotic quality.
From the Saxon hemlic, hymlic.
In Scripture, rendering the Hebrew rosh, a bitter or venomous herb, elsewhere translated gall.
A weed of cultivated ground, springing up in furrows without sowing (Hos 10:4).
Used figuratively of judgment perverted into poison (Amo 6:12).
scriptures: Hos 10:4
They have spoken words, swearing falsely in making a covenant: thus judgment springeth up as hemlock in the furrows of the field.
Amo 6:12
Shall horses run upon the rock? will one plow there with oxen? for ye have turned judgment into gall, and the fruit of righteousness into hemlock:
Amo 5:24
But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.

Lest there should be among you man, or woman, or family, or tribe, whose heart turneth away this day from the LORD our God, to go and serve the gods of these nations; lest there should be among you a root that beareth gall and wormwood;
corruption_summary: Justice is now widely treated as an instrument to be aimed rather than a standard to be kept — which is precisely Amos’s charge, that judgment itself had been turned into gall.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the weaponising of judgment. Both prophets describe societies with functioning legal machinery: courts sat, covenants were made, oaths were sworn, verdicts were handed down. What Amos indicts is not the absence of judgment but its transformation — ye have turned judgment into gall. Law had become the tool by which the strong took the vineyard of the weak, and the very institution appointed to protect the poor was the instrument of their ruin. That is a far more advanced disease than lawlessness, and it is the disease of every sophisticated society, ours included, wherever process is used to grind a man down, or a statute is applied to an enemy and suspended for a friend.

Recover the plain sense: the standard is not that judgment should exist but that it should be just, and Amos supplies the image against which every legal system is to be measured — let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream (Amo 5:24). Water that runs down finds the low places; a mighty stream is not diverted around the powerful. Hosea adds the root: false swearing in the making of covenants. Where a man’s word can be given and withdrawn at convenience, the furrows are already prepared for hemlock, and Moses names the bitter root long before either prophet — a root that beareth gall and wormwood, springing from a heart that turneth away from the LORD (Deu 29:18).
roots_summary: Saxon hemlic, a bitter poison — rendering Hebrew rosh, gall; the crop of a nation that has poisoned its own courts.
roots_lines: Hemlock — Saxon hemlic, a poisonous field herb.
Hebrew rosh, a bitter or venomous plant, elsewhere rendered gall.
Not the American hemlock tree but a rank weed of cultivated ground.
Hos 10:4: it springs in the furrows where covenants are falsely sworn.
Amo 6:12 sets it among impossibilities: horses running on rock, ploughing bare stone.
usage: In both prophets the courts still function — it is the crop that has changed.
Amo 5:24 gives the standard: judgment running down as waters, finding the low places.
Deu 29:18 names the root of gall and wormwood as a heart turning from the LORD.

etymology: From the Latin populus, the poplar tree, through the Old French poplier. A tall, fast-growing tree of the willow family, notable for its pale bark — which is precisely the feature that matters in its chief biblical appearance.
biblical_def: The poplar appears in one of the strangest passages in Genesis: “And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods” (Gen 30:37). Jacob, having agreed with Laban to take the speckled and spotted of the flock as his wages, peels stripes of bark from green rods so that the pale wood shows through in bands, and sets them in the watering troughs before the breeding flocks. It is folk husbandry, and it has puzzled readers for centuries. The decisive point is that Scripture does not endorse the technique — it records it, and then Jacob himself supplies the true explanation. In the next chapter he tells his wives that the angel of God spoke to him in a dream, and that it was God who took away the cattle of their father and gave them to him: God hath not suffered him to hurt me. Jacob employed a superstition; God gave the increase. That is the pattern of his whole life — a man of stratagems, ladders, wrestlings, and bargains, blessed at every turn not because his methods worked but because a covenant held him. The poplar rods stand in the trough as a small monument to how little our contrivances contribute to what God has determined to give.
webster_summary: A tall fast-growing tree of the willow family with pale wood beneath its bark; used by Jacob for the peeled rods set before Laban’s flocks.
webster_full: POPLAR, n. A tree of the genus Populus, of several species, of quick growth and soft white wood.
From the Latin populus, a poplar; Old French poplier.
Distinguished by pale wood lying immediately beneath a darker bark.
Gen 30:37: Jacob pilled white strakes in rods of green poplar.
Some render the Hebrew libneh the storax or white styrax; the name signifies whiteness.
scriptures: And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods.
And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted.
Gen 31:9
Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me.
And he said, Lift up now thine eyes, and see, all the rams which leap upon the cattle are ringstraked, speckled, and grisled: for I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee.
corruption_summary: The passage is used by sceptics to charge Scripture with endorsing folk magic, and by others as a template for technique-driven faith — both ignore that Jacob himself credits the increase entirely to God.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption runs two ways. Sceptics point to the peeled rods and announce that the Bible teaches prenatal influence by visual impression — primitive superstition presented as fact. That misreads the narrative’s method: Scripture constantly records what men did without commending it, and this account carries its own correction two chapters later. In the other direction, some readers take the rods as a model for spiritual technique, as though the right procedure applied with sufficient faith will produce a desired outcome. That is the same error in devotional clothing, and it is the engine of a great deal of popular religion — the formula, the prayer said in the right form, the act performed to secure a result.

Recover the plain sense: the text supplies its own interpretation and it is entirely theocentric. God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me (Gen 31:9), and the angel in the dream shows Jacob that the rams leaping upon the cattle were ringstraked, speckled, and grisled — that is, the increase was in the flock before Jacob ever cut a rod. He was told this expressly so that he should not mistake the cause. Take the lesson honestly, for it cuts at our own contrivances: God frequently blesses His people while they are busy with methods that have nothing to do with the blessing, and afterwards shows them the dream so they will not credit the rods.
roots_summary: Latin populus, poplar — the pale-wooded tree; Jacob’s peeled rods, and God’s increase which owed them nothing.
roots_lines: Poplar — Latin populus; Old French poplier.
Hebrew libneh, from a root signifying white.
Its pale wood beneath the bark is the point of Gen 30:37.
Pilled means peeled; strakes are stripes.
Gen 31:9–12: Jacob credits the increase wholly to God, not to the rods.
usage: Scripture records Jacob’s method without commending it.
The angel’s dream shows the increase was already in the flock.
God often blesses His people amid methods that contribute nothing.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s rendering of the Hebrew ets shemen, literally “tree of oil” — probably the oleaster or wild olive, a hardy tree of dry ground, elsewhere rendered olive tree and pine.
biblical_def: The oil tree stands in one of the great wilderness promises of Isaiah: “I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together” (Isa 41:19). Seven trees are named, and the list is deliberately impossible. The cedar belongs to Lebanon’s heights, the myrtle to well-watered ground, the fir and the box to cool hills — and God says He will set them in the desert, together. Nothing in the verse is agriculture; all of it is creation. And the purpose is stated in the next verse with unusual precision: “That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it” (Isa 41:20). Four verbs of apprehension, piled up, because the whole point of the miracle is that no one could mistake its author. A wilderness does not grow cedars by degrees. The oil tree is a fitting member of the company, for the olive is the tree of oil — of light in the lamp, of anointing for prophet, priest, and king, of healing poured into wounds. God plants in the desert the very tree from which anointing comes, and the desert is where His people were.
webster_summary: The Hebrew “tree of oil,” probably the oleaster or wild olive; one of seven trees God promises to plant in the wilderness.
webster_full: OIL TREE, n. The rendering of the Hebrew ets shemen, a tree yielding oil.
Probably the oleaster, or wild olive, a hardy tree of dry and rocky ground.
The same Hebrew is elsewhere rendered olive tree (1Ki 6:23) and pine branches (Neh 8:15).
Isa 41:19 numbers it among seven trees to be planted in the wilderness.
The olive supplies oil for the lamp, for anointing, and for healing.
scriptures: I will open rivers in high places, and fountains in the midst of the valleys: I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water.
I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together:
That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it.
Isa 35:1
The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
corruption_summary: Promises of wilderness planting are commonly spiritualised into a general optimism about personal circumstances, losing the stated purpose — that men should know the hand of the LORD has done it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The abiding misuse is the reduction of a creation promise to a mood of encouragement. Isa 41:19 is quoted to assure people that their difficult season will improve, which is not false but is very much less than the text says. The verse is one of a series in which God challenges the idols to predict anything at all, and offers as His own credential that He will do what no god and no gardener can — put cedars in a desert. It is a courtroom argument about deity, not a sentiment about hard times.

Recover the plain sense: read verse 20 as the interpretation of verse 19. God does not plant the wilderness so that His people may be comfortable but that they may see, and know, and consider, and understand whose hand it is. The mercy is real, and it is aimed at knowledge of Him. That reframes how a Christian should read his own deliverances: the question after a rescue is not merely am I better off but what has this taught me of the Holy One of Israel? And note the setting — verse 18 opens rivers in high places and fountains in the midst of the valleys, for God waters before He plants. The desert does not become fertile so that trees may grow; the trees are set, and the water is given, and the whole arrangement is a witness.
roots_summary: Hebrew ets shemen, tree of oil — the wild olive; planted in the desert so that men should know whose hand did it.
roots_lines: Oil tree — Hebrew ets shemen, literally tree of oil.
Probably the oleaster or wild olive, hardy on dry ground.
The same Hebrew is rendered olive tree and pine elsewhere.
One of seven trees promised to the wilderness in Isa 41:19.
Isa 41:20 states the purpose: that they may see, know, consider, and understand.
usage: The list is deliberately impossible — cedar and myrtle set together in a desert.
Isa 41:20 makes knowledge of God, not comfort, the aim of the miracle.
The olive is the tree of the lamp, the anointing, and the healing oil.

etymology: From the Greek sykaminos, the black mulberry tree — distinguished in the Gospels from sykomoraia, the sycomore fig which Zacchaeus climbed. A tree proverbial for the depth and tenacity of its roots.
biblical_def: The sycamine occurs once, and the occasion is one of the most misread sayings of our Lord. The apostles had said, “Increase our faith” (Luk 17:5) — a request that sounds pious and contains a mistake. Christ answers: “If ye had faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye might say unto this sycamine tree, Be thou plucked up by the root, and be thou planted in the sea; and it should obey you” (Luk 17:6). Two impossibilities are joined. The sycamine was proverbial for roots so deep and tough that it was reckoned nearly impossible to shift; and no tree is planted in the sea and lives. Note carefully what the Lord does not say. He does not say get more faith and you will manage it. He says if you had faith as a grain of mustard seed — the smallest of seeds — the thing would be done. The disciples asked for a greater quantity; He redirects them to the nature of the thing. Faith is not a substance of which one accumulates enough to reach a threshold; it is a hand laid on the arm of God, and the smallest true hold on an omnipotent arm is sufficient. The context sharpens it further: the request came immediately after the command to forgive a brother seven times in a day, which the disciples evidently thought needed more faith than they possessed. Perhaps it does need what no quantity supplies.
webster_summary: The black mulberry tree, proverbial for its deep and tenacious roots; used by our Lord to teach that faith is measured by its object, not its quantity.
webster_full: SYCAMINE, n. The black mulberry tree.
From the Greek sykaminos, the mulberry.
Distinguished from the sycomore (Greek sykomoraia), the fig-mulberry of Luk 19:4.
Noted among the ancients for roots of unusual depth and tenacity.
Luk 17:6: the tree our Lord names as the type of the immovable.
scriptures: Luk 17:4
And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him.
Luk 17:5
And the apostles said unto the Lord, Increase our faith.
Luk 17:6
And the Lord said, If ye had faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye might say unto this sycamine tree, Be thou plucked up by the root, and be thou planted in the sea; and it should obey you.

And Jesus said unto them, Because of your unbelief: for verily I say unto you, If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you.
corruption_summary: The saying is universally inverted into a doctrine of faith as a measurable force — enough of it moves trees and mountains — when our Lord’s whole point is that quantity is not the category.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is faith conceived as a quantity, and it is the engine of the entire word-of-faith and prosperity movement. On that reading, faith is a substance a believer accumulates and directs; results are proportional to the amount; and failure therefore indicts the supply. The pastoral consequences are cruel, since every unanswered prayer becomes evidence against the one praying, and the sick and the bereaved are told, in effect, that they did not believe hard enough. The dictionary rejects the doctrine outright. It cannot survive Luk 17:6, where the disciples ask precisely for an increase and are answered with the smallest of seeds. Christ’s reply is not you need more but you have mistaken the thing.

Recover the plain sense: faith saves and moves because of what it lays hold of. A weak hand on a strong rope is safer than a strong hand on a rotten one, and Scripture is full of small faith honoured — Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief, the trembling touch of a garment hem, a thief’s dying sentence. Nor is the promise a licence to relocate shrubbery: our Lord speaks in the settled hyperbole of the rabbis, naming an unmovable tree and an impossible planting to say that nothing standing in the way of God’s purpose can resist Him. And remember the setting. The apostles asked for more faith because they had just been told to forgive a brother seven times in one day. Forgiving like that is the tree with the deep roots.
roots_summary: Greek sykaminos, the black mulberry — the deep-rooted tree; our Lord’s figure for what the smallest true faith can move.
roots_lines: Sycamine — Greek sykaminos, the black mulberry.
Distinct from the sycomore fig of Luk 19:4, which Zacchaeus climbed.
Proverbially deep-rooted and hard to uproot.
Luk 17:6 joins two impossibilities: uprooting it, and planting it in the sea.
Mat 17:20 uses the same mustard-seed figure of a mountain.
usage: The disciples asked for more; Christ answered with the smallest seed.
Faith is measured by its object, not by its quantity.
The setting is Luk 17:4 — forgiving a brother seven times in a day.

etymology: From the Old French lie, the sediment of wine, of Celtic origin. The lees are the dregs that settle at the bottom of a wine vessel; wine left long upon its lees grows strong and clear, but the same stillness that refines good wine sours bad.
biblical_def: Lees are wine-sediment, and Scripture makes brilliant double use of the image. On the one hand, wine aged upon the lees is the finest wine, and so it appears in the great banquet promise: “in this mountain shall the LORD of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined” (Isa 25:6). Note well refined — the wine has rested long and been drawn off clear. On the other hand, the same settling describes a soul that has never been disturbed. Moab “hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel” (Jer 48:11), and the verse ends devastatingly: therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed. Moab was never poured out, never uprooted, never carried captive — and so never changed. Undisturbed prosperity preserved him exactly as he was. Zephaniah applies the same figure to Jerusalem: God will “search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil” (Zep 1:12). That is practical atheism in a sentence — not the denial of God’s existence but of His activity, the settled conviction of a comfortable man that heaven is indifferent.
webster_summary: The sediment or dregs of wine, settling at the bottom of the vessel; used both of wine long refined and of a soul left undisturbed and therefore unchanged.
webster_full: LEES, n. plural. The grosser parts of liquor which settle at the bottom; dregs; sediment.
From the Old French lie, dregs; of Celtic origin.
Wine left upon the lees and then drawn off is strengthened and clarified (Isa 25:6).
To be settled on the lees is to remain long undisturbed in one vessel (Jer 48:11).
Figuratively, of a man grown thick and unchanged through ease.
scriptures: Isa 25:6
And in this mountain shall the LORD of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined.

Moab hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither hath he gone into captivity: therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed.
Zep 1:12

And it shall come to pass at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil.
God shall hear, and afflict them, even he that abideth of old. Selah. Because they have no changes, therefore they fear not God.
corruption_summary: An untroubled life is read as a sign of divine favour, when Jeremiah names undisturbed ease as the very reason Moab’s taste remained in him and his scent was not changed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the equation of ease with blessing. It is nearly universal, and it is refuted in one of the sharpest verses in the prophets. Moab had everything a man could pray for — at ease from his youth, never emptied from vessel to vessel, never gone into captivity — and Jeremiah presents the whole record as an indictment. The unbroken calm did not sanctify him; it fixed him. Therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed. The very absence of upheaval preserved every fault he had at twenty into his old age. The Psalmist says the same of men who have no changes: therefore they fear not God (Psa 55:19).

Recover the plain sense: God empties His people from vessel to vessel on purpose. The disturbances a Christian resents — the move, the loss, the illness, the reversal — are frequently the pouring that keeps him from thickening on his lees. This is not a doctrine that romanticises suffering, nor does it promise that every trouble improves a man; the fool in the mortar is answer enough to that. But it does forbid reading a smooth life as a certificate. Zephaniah names the end state precisely: men settled on their lees say in their heart The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil — a God who is real, and irrelevant. Against that, set Isa 25:6, where the wine on the lees is well refined, kept long and then drawn off clear. There is a settling that ruins and a settling that matures, and the difference is whether the vessel was ever tipped.
roots_summary: Old French lie, sediment — the dregs beneath the wine; the figure of ease that thickens a soul, and of wine long refined.
roots_lines: Lees — Old French lie, the sediment of wine.
Wine long upon the lees and drawn off clear is the strongest (Isa 25:6).
Jer 48:11: Moab settled on his lees, never emptied from vessel to vessel.
The result: his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed.
Zep 1:12: settled men say the LORD will do neither good nor evil.
usage: The same stillness refines good wine and ruins a man.
Psa 55:19: because they have no changes, therefore they fear not God.
Zep 1:12 defines practical atheism — not denying God, but denying He acts.

etymology: From the Norse dregg, sediment. The dregs are what lies at the bottom of a cup — the thick, bitter residue drunk last by the one who empties it, and therefore Scripture’s figure for the uttermost of wrath.
biblical_def: The dregs are the bottom of the cup, and Scripture builds one of its most terrible images upon them. “For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them” (Psa 75:8). Two things are asserted: the cup is in God’s hand, and the wicked will drink it to the very bottom, wringing out the last of it. Isaiah turns the same figure upon Jerusalem — “thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling” (Isa 51:17), a city staggering like a drunkard under judgment. And then comes one of the great gospel reversals of the Old Testament. God says to that same city: “Behold, I have taken out of thine hand the cup of trembling, even the dregs of the cup of my fury; thou shalt no more drink it again” (Isa 51:22). The cup is not diluted, nor waived, nor set aside — it is taken out of her hand, which means someone else must hold it. The New Testament shows who. In Gethsemane the Son prays, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me, and then drinks it; and on the cross He does not stop partway. The dregs are the point. A Saviour who drank most of the cup would leave His people the bitterest part; He wrung it out.
webster_summary: The sediment at the bottom of a cup; the last and bitterest portion, and hence in Scripture the uttermost measure of divine wrath.
webster_full: DREGS, n. plural. The sediment of liquors; lees; grounds; feculence.
From the Norse dregg, sediment.
Waste or worthless matter; the most despicable part of anything.
In Scripture, the last and bitterest portion of the cup of wrath (Psa 75:8).
To wring out the dregs is to drain the vessel utterly.
scriptures: Psa 75:8

For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them.
Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem, which hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out.

Thus saith thy Lord the LORD, and thy God that pleadeth the cause of his people, Behold, I have taken out of thine hand the cup of trembling, even the dregs of the cup of my fury; thou shalt no more drink it again:
And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
corruption_summary: Penal substitution is widely dismissed as unworthy of God, but the cup imagery is Scripture’s own, and it is the same cup — taken from His people’s hand and drunk by the Son.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the rejection of substitutionary wrath. It is now common to hear that a Father punishing a Son is unjust, even monstrous, and that the cross must instead be read as solidarity, example, or the exposure of violence. The dictionary rejects this and holds with the confession that Christ bore the wrath of God in the room and stead of His people. Note that the cup image is not a later theological construction imposed on the text; it is the Bible’s own vocabulary, running from Psa 75:8 through Isa 51 to Gethsemane, where our Lord Himself names what He is about to drink. Strip the wrath out and Isa 51:22 becomes unintelligible — God takes the cup out of thine hand, and it must then be in someone’s.

Recover the plain sense: the objection misconceives the parties. This is not an angry deity venting upon an unwilling third party, but the Son of God who volunteered before the world was, one in essence with the Father, laying down His life of Himself — no man taketh it from me. The Trinity is not divided at Calvary; it is unanimous. And take the comfort the dregs are there to give. Because He wrung the cup out, there is nothing left in it for those who are His. Rom 8:1 follows necessarily: there is therefore now no condemnation, not because condemnation was waived, but because it was drunk.
roots_summary: Norse dregg, sediment — the bitter bottom of the cup; wrath drunk to the last, and taken out of His people’s hand.
roots_lines: Dregs — Norse dregg, sediment; the thick residue of a cup.
Psa 75:8: the cup is in the hand of the LORD, and the wicked wring out the dregs.
Isa 51:17: Jerusalem staggering, having drunk the dregs of the cup of trembling.
Isa 51:22: God takes the cup out of thine hand — so another must hold it.
Mat 26:39: the Son prays over the cup and then drinks it.
usage: The cup imagery is Scripture’s own vocabulary, not a later theological import.
Isa 51:22 requires a substitute: the cup is taken from one hand into another.
Because the dregs were wrung out, there is nothing left in the cup for His people.

etymology: From the Latin conficere, to make up or prepare — con, together, and facere, to make. A confection is a compound prepared by art, several ingredients tempered into one; the modern restriction to sweets is a narrowing of a much wider old sense.
biblical_def: The word belongs to the holy anointing perfume: “And thou shalt make it a perfume, a confection after the art of the apothecary, tempered together, pure and holy” (Exo 30:35). The ingredients were named exactly — stacte, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense, of each a like weight (Exo 30:34) — and the compounding was skilled work, after the art of the apothecary. God did not despise craftsmanship in the things of His house; He specified it. But the passage closes with a prohibition as strict as the recipe: “as for the perfume which thou shalt make, ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof: it shall be unto thee holy for the LORD” (Exo 30:37), and whoever made the like of it, to smell thereto, was to be cut off from his people. The scent was reserved. An Israelite could smell it in only one place, and the moment it reached him he knew where he was. Here is the doctrine in the perfume: God appoints the means of His worship, specifies them, and fences them, and the sin named is not neglect but imitation — taking what was given for the sanctuary and making a private version for personal pleasure. Note also the word tempered, which the margin renders salted. Even the perfume was salted, as every meat offering was seasoned with the salt of the covenant.
webster_summary: A compound prepared by art from several ingredients tempered together; in Exodus, the holy perfume of the sanctuary, whose composition no man might imitate.
webster_full: CONFECTION, n. A compound or composition; a preparation of several ingredients mixed together.
From the Latin conficere, to make up, from con and facere, to make.
In pharmacy, a soft solid medicine compounded of various materials.
A sweetmeat; the modern and narrower sense of the word.
Exo 30:35: the holy perfume, a confection after the art of the apothecary.
scriptures: And the LORD said unto Moses, Take unto thee sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum; these sweet spices with pure frankincense: of each shall there be a like weight:
And thou shalt make it a perfume, a confection after the art of the apothecary, tempered together, pure and holy:
And as for the perfume which thou shalt make, ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof: it shall be unto thee holy for the LORD.
Whosoever shall make like unto that, to smell thereto, shall even be cut off from his people.
corruption_summary: Worship is now designed to whatever will move an audience, on the assumption that God has left the manner to our discretion — a principle Exo 30 explicitly denies by fencing even a fragrance.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the notion that God has regulated the object of worship and left the manner open. On that assumption, sincerity and effectiveness become the only tests, and whatever gathers or moves a congregation is permissible. Exodus will not allow it. God specified four spices by name and by weight, required them tempered by skilled art, declared the result holy, and then attached the penalty of being cut off to any man who reproduced the scent for himself. If a fragrance was fenced this closely, the notion that the substance of worship is at our discretion cannot stand. The same book records Nadab and Abihu offering strange fire which he commanded them not, and the fire that came out from the LORD.

Recover the plain sense: God is not indifferent to how He is approached, and the reformed principle that worship is to be governed by what He has appointed is not a narrowing of liberty but a protection of it. Notice what the fencing accomplished. Because the perfume existed nowhere else, its scent was unmistakable; an Israelite who caught it knew he was at the tabernacle and nowhere else. A worship that borrows every method of the surrounding culture has no scent of its own, and men can no longer tell by it where they are. Notice too that God commanded excellence — after the art of the apothecary. Regulated worship is not careless worship; it is skilled work done within appointed bounds.
roots_summary: Latin conficere, to make up — a compound tempered by art; the sanctuary perfume no man might imitate.
roots_lines: Confection — Latin con + facere, to make together.
A compound of several ingredients, not necessarily sweet; the modern sense is narrowed.
Exo 30:34: stacte, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense, of each a like weight.
Tempered together — the margin reads salted, as the meat offering was.
Exo 30:37–38: to copy the scent for private use was to be cut off.
usage: God specified the ingredients, the weights, and the craftsmanship.
The sin named is imitation for private pleasure, not neglect.
A fenced fragrance meant an Israelite always knew where he was when he smelled it.

etymology: From the Saxon har, grey or white with age — the same word as in hoary and hoar head. Hoar frost is the white rime that whitens a surface as age whitens hair; the two senses meet in the one Saxon root.
biblical_def: Hoar frost is the white rime of morning, and Scripture uses it for the manna and for the majesty of God in winter. In the wilderness, “when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground” (Exo 16:14). The comparison is exact and humbling: God’s daily provision for a nation looked like frost — small, white, granular, and lying loose on the sand. Israel’s reaction was a question, “It is manna: for they wist not what it was” (Exo 16:15), the Hebrew man hu meaning simply what is it? They named their bread after their own bewilderment, and ate it for forty years. The Psalmist takes the same frost as a token of God’s effortless power: “He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes” (Psa 147:16). Ashes are scattered with a flick of the hand; so God distributes winter. And the word’s other family, the hoar head, gives the ageing believer one of the most tender promises in Isaiah: “even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear” (Isa 46:4). The same whiteness lies on the wilderness at dawn and on the head of an old saint, and God claims responsibility for both.
webster_summary: The white frost or rime that whitens the ground; from the Saxon word for grey with age, which also gives hoar head and hoary.
webster_full: HOAR, adj. White; whitish; grey with age; as, hoar hairs.
From the Saxon har, hoary, grey.
HOAR FROST, n. The white particles of ice formed by the congelation of dew; rime.
The hoar head is the head whitened by age, a crown of glory if found in the way of righteousness (Pro 16:31).
Exo 16:14 likens the manna to hoar frost lying on the ground.
scriptures: And when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground.
And when the children of Israel saw it, they said one to another, It is manna: for they wist not what it was. And Moses said unto them, This is the bread which the LORD hath given you to eat.
He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes.
Isa 46:4
And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you.
corruption_summary: Daily provision is now expected to look impressive, so the ordinary means by which God actually feeds His people — small, plain, and repeated — go unrecognised, exactly as the manna did.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The abiding temptation is contempt for the ordinary. Israel’s bread from heaven — a genuine and continuous miracle, sustaining perhaps two million people for forty years — looked like frost on the sand, and had to be gathered every morning before the sun melted it, in the same quantity, by every household, with nothing left over. Within a short time they were weary of it: our soul loatheth this light bread. That is the settled human reaction to daily grace. We ask God for provision and then despise it for arriving in an unremarkable form, and we are far more interested in the sea opening than in the frost that lay every single morning for four decades.

Recover the plain sense: God’s ordinary means are His chief means. The preached word, the Lord’s table, the reading of Scripture, prayer, and the fellowship of the saints are the manna — small, plain, repeated, and easily despised, and there is no other food. Our Lord took the manna as the figure of Himself: I am that bread of life. Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead. The frost on the ground pointed to Him all along. And let the aged saint take the other half of the word: the same God who scattered the hoar frost like ashes says even to hoar hairs will I carry you. He who fed them daily in the wilderness does not set down His people when their own heads turn white.
roots_summary: Saxon har, grey with age — white rime; the look of the manna, and the promise to hoar hairs.
roots_lines: Hoar frost — Saxon har, grey or white; the rime of morning.
The same root gives hoary and the hoar head of age.
Exo 16:14: the manna lay small and white, as hoar frost on the ground.
Manna is from man hu, “what is it?” — Israel named it from their bewilderment.
Psa 147:16: He scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes — winter dealt with a flick of the hand.
usage: The greatest sustained miracle in the Old Testament looked like frost.
Manna had to be gathered daily, in measure, and melted in the sun.
Isa 46:4 carries the same whiteness from the wilderness to the aged believer’s head.

etymology: From the Old French doel, grief, and that from the Latin dolere, to grieve or suffer pain — the root of dolour and condole. Full of grief; expressing or causing sorrow.
biblical_def: Doleful appears twice, and both instances are sounds of desolation. In the oracle against Babylon, “their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there” (Isa 13:21) — the Hebrew is literally howling things, creatures whose cry is a wail, filling the rooms where a court once sat. And in Micah, the sound comes from the people themselves: “In that day shall one take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, and say, We be utterly spoiled: he hath changed the portion of my people” (Mic 2:4). The Hebrew here is a striking construction, a wailing of wailings, grief piled upon its own word. What is being mourned is instructive — he hath changed the portion of my people. Micah had been indicting men who coveted fields and took them, who oppressed a man and his house, and the judgment answers the sin exactly: those who moved the boundaries of other men’s portions find their own portion changed and divided among strangers. Scripture does not treat such lament as unbelief. It records it, gives it words, and sets whole books in its key. But it also refuses to leave the reader there: the same prophet who writes the wailing of wailings ends his book asking Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity?
webster_summary: Full of grief; sorrowful; expressing or causing dolour. Used of the howling creatures of a ruined city and of a lamentation piled upon itself.
webster_full: DOLEFUL, adj. Sorrowful; expressing grief; as a doleful whine.
Melancholy; afflicted; full of grief.
Dismal; impressing sorrow; gloomy; as a doleful place.
From the Old French doel, grief; Latin dolere, to grieve; whence dolour.
Isa 13:21: doleful creatures, in the Hebrew literally howling things.
scriptures: But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there.
Mic 2:4

In that day shall one take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, and say, We be utterly spoiled: he hath changed the portion of my people: how hath he removed it from me! turning away he hath divided our fields.
Mic 2:2
And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.
Mic 7:18
Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.
corruption_summary: Lament has been squeezed out of ordinary church life by an expectation of relentless positivity, leaving grieving believers without permitted language — though Scripture supplies whole books of it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the demand for perpetual brightness. A great deal of modern religious culture has no settled place for sorrow that does not resolve quickly: songs are chosen for their lift, testimonies for their happy ending, and the believer in prolonged grief learns to answer fine because the alternative unsettles the room. Scripture is far broader. Roughly a third of the Psalter is lament, an entire book is named Lamentations, Job sits in ashes for chapters, and the prophets wail. Micah’s doleful lamentation is a wailing of wailings — grief doubled in the grammar itself. God gave His people this vocabulary; a church that will not use it has silenced part of inspired speech.

Recover the plain sense: lament is not the opposite of faith but one of its languages, and it is addressed to God rather than merely about circumstances. Note also what Micah mourns: he hath changed the portion of my people, a judgment fitted precisely to the sin of Mic 2:2, where men coveted fields and took them by violence. The lament is honest about deserving. That is what distinguishes biblical grief from mere despair — it tells the truth about God’s justice while it weeps. And it does not end there. The prophet who wrote the wailing of wailings closes his book with Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage?
roots_summary: Latin dolere, to grieve — full of sorrow; the howling of a ruined city and the wailing of wailings.
roots_lines: Doleful — Old French doel, grief; Latin dolere, to suffer pain.
Kin to dolour, condole, and indolent (literally, feeling no pain).
Isa 13:21: the Hebrew for doleful creatures is literally howling things.
Mic 2:4: a doleful lamentation is in Hebrew a wailing of wailings.
The judgment answers the sin: those who moved others’ portions lose their own.
usage: Scripture supplies whole books in this key; a church without lament has lost inspired speech.
Biblical lament is honest about deserving — Mic 2:4 answers Mic 2:2 exactly.
Micah’s wailing ends in Mic 7:18: Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity?

etymology: A phrase rendering the Hebrew chemdath nashim — chemdah, that which is desired or precious, and nashim, women. It occurs once, in Daniel’s prophecy of the wilful king, and its exact reference has been debated since the earliest commentators.
biblical_def: The phrase belongs to Daniel’s portrait of the king who does according to his will: “Neither shall he regard the God of his fathers, nor the desire of women, nor regard any god: for he shall magnify himself above all” (Dan 11:37). The structure of the verse is the key to it. Three things are named that the king disregards, and the outer two are plainly religious — the God of his fathers and any god — with the phrase sitting between them. That placement has led most sober interpreters to take the desire of women as a deity or object of devotion rather than a comment on the king’s domestic life: either a god particularly adored by women, such as Tammuz, whom Ezekiel saw women weeping for at the gate of the LORD’s house, or the hope of Hebrew women to bear the Messiah. Others take it simply of natural affection, a man so consumed by self-exaltation that he has no room for ordinary human love. What is beyond dispute is the verse’s conclusion, which the whole sentence drives toward: he shall magnify himself above all. Whatever the phrase names, it is one more thing sacrificed to self-magnification, and Daniel’s wilful king is recognisable in every age — a man who will give up his God, his gods, and his affections rather than give up himself.
webster_summary: A phrase in Daniel’s prophecy of the wilful king, denoting something he disregards — most probably an object of devotion, and set between two plainly religious terms.
webster_full: DESIRE, n. That which is desired; the object of longing.
Rendering the Hebrew chemdah, a precious or desirable thing.
The phrase the desire of women occurs only at Dan 11:37.
Anciently understood by many of a deity peculiarly honoured by women, as Tammuz (Eze 8:14).
By others, of the hope of Hebrew women to be mother of the promised seed.
scriptures: And the king shall do according to his will; and he shall exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak marvellous things against the God of gods, and shall prosper till the indignation be accomplished: for that that is determined shall be done.
Neither shall he regard the God of his fathers, nor the desire of women, nor regard any god: for he shall magnify himself above all.
Eze 8:14
Then he brought me to the door of the gate of the LORD'S house which was toward the north; and, behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz.
Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God.
corruption_summary: Obscure prophetic phrases are routinely turned into confident charts of current events, and this one has carried a long train of speculation about the identity and habits of Antichrist.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is speculative prophecy. A phrase occurring once, whose reference the ancient commentators already disputed, has been made to yield detailed conclusions about the personal life, nationality, and religion of a coming Antichrist, and each generation’s identification has aged badly. The dictionary rejects the whole method. Scripture’s obscure places are to be read in the light of its plain places, not the reverse, and a doctrine erected on a disputed clause is a house built on the one stone in the wall no one can identify. Where the Reformers and the Puritans read Dan 11 they were far more concerned with the character it describes than with dating its fulfilment.

Recover the plain sense: the verse is not obscure about its main assertion. He shall magnify himself above all — that is the wilful king’s defining act, and Paul describes the same figure in terms that leave nothing to guess: he opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped (2Th 2:4). What Daniel gives us is a portrait of self-exaltation so complete that it discards inherited religion, foreign religion, and human affection alike, keeping nothing that might rival the self. That description is useful to every reader now, whatever the phrase in the middle means, because the spirit it describes is not confined to one man at the end of history. Every soul knows something of the impulse to keep the self at the centre, and the antidote is the mind that was in Christ Jesus, who being in the form of God made Himself of no reputation.
roots_summary: Hebrew chemdath nashim, the desire of women — a disputed phrase in Dan 11:37, framed by two religious terms and driving to self-magnification.
roots_lines: Desire of women — Hebrew chemdath nashim, from chemdah, a desirable thing.
Occurs only at Dan 11:37, in the prophecy of the wilful king.
Set between the God of his fathers and any god — both plainly religious terms.
Anciently referred by many to Tammuz, wept for by women in Eze 8:14.
By others to the hope of Hebrew women to bear the promised seed.
usage: Read the phrase by its frame: the outer two terms are objects of worship.
The verse’s undisputed point is he shall magnify himself above all.
2Th 2:4 describes the same self-exalting figure in plain terms.
